name: Victor Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have spent years answering missed-parcel calls and chats at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and handle a normal complaint at about the pace of the other experienced agents; I do not supervise anyone. My wage is typical for this job. I use the approved AI summary now and then after a colleague checks it, but I keep the original delivery scan open.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is waiting when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ines works regular hours at a neighbourhood laundry, and our grown daughter and son run their own households. We rent the flat and have about four months of expenses saved, with some other contact centres nearby. We talk about easing off work one day, but have not worked out what income would replace either wage. I like finding the actual parcel more than closing a neat-looking case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the desk that a quicker parcel summary is useful if we still check the delivery scan. I will not call a case finished because a green box says it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my usual shifts and Ines’s laundry wage to continue. Four months saved is enough to handle a broken cooker, but I do not want to spend it on a shortcut we have not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep handling missed-parcel calls and reading the last scan to the customer. In the first year of small change, if the centre offers a paid Saturday cover shift, I will put that extra wage into the rent account instead of buying a new television.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job, with the ordinary rent still in mind. A tidy screen cannot tell me whether the parcel crossed the right doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which scan made you stop a refund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a parcel had the right street but the wrong flat number. I called the depot after reading the paper scan, and the driver found it upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines and I would leave the four-month reserve alone unless a real bill or wage gap arrives. Our children have their own bills; I do not count their earnings as ours.

say: I would check **delivery scans** before closing a missed-parcel case.
I would use a **faster summary** only beside the original record.
think: I expect my **usual shifts** and Ines’s laundry pay to continue.
I keep **four months saved** for a real bill or wage gap.
do: Keep answering **missed-parcel calls** and reading original scans to customers.
Save any **paid Saturday cover wage** for rent rather than buying a television.
feel: **Calm** about work, mindful of ordinary rent.
S0.quote: A tidy screen cannot tell me whether the parcel crossed the right doorstep.
fieldNote: His **ordinary wage** and four-month reserve make the mild picture manageable.
He uses **AI occasionally** but checks the actual delivery scan.
The extra saving depends on an **offered paid shift**, not guaranteed overtime.

steps.text: Keep handling missed-parcel calls and read original delivery scans
Save extra Saturday wage for rent only if paid cover is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that software will answer the easy tracking questions first. I would ask the supervisor to show the paid rota beside the number of chats the new system closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience may keep me on parcels that are actually lost, but the short calls help fill a full week. If those hours go, four months saved will not make a lower wage equal to this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will learn the new AI route-check screen on ten old wrong-address cases during paid time, but only if a senior agent can show me where to log a bad match. If simple chats move in the first year, I will keep my current calls and compare posted paid depot-counter hours with my written weekly wage; I will apply only if those hours cover rent and bills after the bus fare, and stay here until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the weekly hours, though I can learn a tool that someone has tested. A faster queue is no bargain if the paid week gets shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in the route test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong flat numbers, not just how quickly the route screen gives an answer. The depot counter would have to let me ask a driver about the actual parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a counter opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines and I would compare the full week on the posting with our rent and utility payments. A better hourly rate would mean little if it came with only two afternoon shifts.

say: I would ask for a **written paid rota** beside automated chat totals.
I would keep **wrong-address cases** visible when the route tool is judged.
think: I may retain **lost-parcel work** because I know the depot calls.
I cannot replace **lost weekly hours** with a four-month reserve.
do: Learn the **AI route-check screen** on ten old cases during paid time if a senior agent shows error logging.
Keep **paid parcel calls** while comparing written weekly pay and posted depot-counter hours.
Apply when **simple chats move** for posted paid counter only on written rent-and-bill-covering weekly pay/hours after fare; stay until signed.
feel: **Anxious** about shorter paid weeks, willing to test proven tools.
S1.quote: A faster queue is no bargain if the paid week gets shorter.
fieldNote: His **new screen practice** is paid learning beyond occasional summary use.
The counter alternative needs a **full paid week**, not an attractive hourly rate.
He keeps the **current wage** until a suitable offer is signed.

steps.text: Learn new AI route-check screen on ten old cases during paid time with error logging shown
Keep paid parcel calls and compare written weekly pay with posted depot-counter hours
Apply when simple chats move: posted paid counter, written rent/bills-covering weekly pay/hours after fare
Stay on paid calls until suitable counter offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my coworkers that full thinking AI by 2028 could settle a tracking complaint before I take the call. The robots for hands-on work come around 2031, but that does not give the phone desk three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our paid call rota to shrink sharply, perhaps enough to lose my own week. Four months saved gives us time to look at some nearby centres, yet Ines’s wage alone will not cover the flat for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will put the planned new television on hold and check two posted paid parcel-intake jobs near the bus route. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I will take an intake shift only after a signed offer states weekly wages and hours covering rent and bills after fare, with a start time I can reach on the first bus; I will keep any current paid calls until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed at the thought of a full paid week disappearing. Four months of rent money is a bridge, not a second job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an intake shift unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether an intake worker has to lift bulky parcels alone. I can move a normal box, but I would not accept a shift that expects unsafe lifting without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the television wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The existing television still works, so Ines and I can wait. We would not ask our grown children to finance an uncertain counter job.

say: I would separate **2028 phone risk** from robots reaching physical work around 2031.
I would ask for **posted paid intake** with real weekly hours.
think: I expect my **paid call week** could disappear quickly.
I know **four months saved** and Ines’s wage cannot carry rent indefinitely.
do: Delay the **new television** while the current one works.
Inspect two posted **paid intake jobs** near the bus and reject unsafe solo lifting.
Move after call loss only on **signed written offer** with weekly pay/hours covering rent and bills after fare and first-bus access.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible loss of his full paid week.
S2.quote: Four months of rent money is a bridge, not a second job.
fieldNote: The **television delay** is feasible because the old set still works.
His **lifting check** is a conditional safety question, not a blanket refusal of intake work.
The **signed offer** must cover weekly bills after fare and a usable first bus.

steps.text: Delay buying new television while the old set works
Inspect two posted paid parcel-intake jobs near bus route; reject unsafe solo lifting
Keep current paid calls until a suitable intake offer is signed
Move after calls end on signed written weekly pay/hours covering rent/bills after fare, with first-bus access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets the depot show which human parcel checks still get paid. Thinking AGI reaches our calls by 2031, while robots that handle physical parcels follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can improve at disputed deliveries while the centre still pays me, but I do not think a better headset title guarantees hours. Ines and I need to know whether a counter wage would carry the same monthly rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I will keep taking the paid complaint shifts and ask the depot supervisor to let me shadow one parcel discrepancy during a paid afternoon, if the rota can cover my calls. I will set aside the pay from one extra Saturday shift each quarter if that shift is offered. If calls fall in the first year after 2031, I will apply for a posted paid depot-counter role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills after bus fare; I will leave only after a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the years ahead, but there is time to check real work. I can practise a disputed parcel, but I cannot practise a missing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority must a counter worker have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor whether the counter can reopen a mistaken delivery or must send the customer back to a phone queue. I would not move for a title that cannot correct the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ines test the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would add the bus fare and our rent to the same sheet as the posting. We would not turn the four-month reserve into a promise that an unpaid shadow day pays us.

say: I would ask which **paid parcel checks** remain before calling a counter role a solution.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from physical robots around 2034.
think: I may improve **dispute skills** while the present desk pays me.
I cannot assume a **counter title** comes with full paid hours.
do: Keep **paid complaint shifts** and shadow one parcel discrepancy on paid time only if rota cover is available.
Save one **extra Saturday wage** per quarter only if that shift is offered.
Apply after 2031 cuts for **posted paid depot work** with correction authority, written after-fare rent-and-bill-covering weekly pay/hours; leave after signing.
feel: **Anxious** about future hours, steadier with time to inspect.
S3.quote: I can practise a disputed parcel, but I cannot practise a missing wage.
fieldNote: The **paid shadow** depends on cover for his existing calls.
The counter must have **reopening authority** as well as enough weekly pay.
He saves **extra wages** only if a paid Saturday shift is offered.

steps.text: Keep paid complaint calls and shadow one discrepancy only on covered paid time
Save one extra Saturday wage quarterly only if offered
Apply after 2031 cuts: posted paid counter, correction authority, written rent/bills-covering pay/hours after fare
Leave paid calls only after suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell friends that a decade is time to keep earning and write down what the household actually needs. Full thinking AGI reaches my calls by 2036, and hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer shifts, but Ines and I have not verified any income that could replace my weekly wage. Four months saved is useful for a gap, not a date on a retirement calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep my paid call rota and sit with Ines each year over rent, utilities, our wages and any verified later-life income. In the first year after 2036, if calls fall and we still need my wage, I will seek posted paid customer-counter work I can reach; I will move only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering our bills after fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy about what a paid week looks like ten years away, but the next few years are workable. Turning sixty-eight will not put a wage in the rent envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would let you reduce nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the weekly wage and hours before choosing fewer nights. If a number for later-life income is unverified, it does not go in our rent calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the counter last through robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the depot whether a counter worker still handles actual returned parcels when robots arrive around 2039. I cannot call the counter permanently safe just because it has a door.

say: I would use the **decade** to compare actual household income with bills.
I would separate **2036 phone change** from physical robots around 2039.
think: I may want **fewer shifts** at 68, but no replacement income is verified.
I treat **four months saved** as a short bridge, not retirement pay.
do: Keep **paid call shifts** and review bills with Ines against wages and verified later-life income each year.
Seek **reachable posted paid counter** if 2036 calls fall and wages remain needed; move on signed written bill-covering weekly pay/hours after fare.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, stable enough now to calculate.
S4.quote: Turning sixty-eight will not put a wage in the rent envelope.
fieldNote: He makes **no pension assumption**; later-life income must be verified.
The **wage-needed and calls-fall** conditions both gate a job search.
Physical robots arrive **around 2039**, after thinking AGI reaches the phone desk.

steps.text: Keep paid calls and review bills with Ines against verified later-life income yearly
Seek reachable posted paid counter if calls fall after 2036 and wages remain needed
Move only on signed written weekly pay/hours covering bills after fare

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my paid headset work could go before I can see a full week of another job. Four months saved buys a search but not a new wage. I would need written shift notice and a posted paid role with hours and pay that cover our rent and bills after the bus fare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want the weekly pay written down before I trade a headset for a counter. An hourly rate on a noticeboard does not tell Ines and me what comes through the door on Friday.

headlineQuote: I want the weekly pay written down before I trade a headset for a counter.
portrait: Victor is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling and typical pay on missed-parcel calls.
He uses **AI occasionally**, after a colleague checks it, and trusts original delivery scans.
Victor and Ines rent with **four months saved** and some nearby centres; their grown children have separate households.
He compares **whole-week pay** before any move and has no verified income plan for stopping work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his paid headset work before another full week is available.
whatWouldHelp: **Written shift notice** and posted paid work with after-fare rent-and-bill-covering weekly wages and hours would help.
